Agree with Rasmr on part of this -

E.g. there eventually should be a point where you are willing to sell

But, the main point I disagree on is that “buying and holding” is a bad strategy.

It’s only a bad strategy if you either:

a) don’t really believe in the meme

Or

b) you’re not bullish on the direction of the broader market

The issue we have is that there are so many people who hype up a meme like it’s a generational narrative and somehow within 24 hours are like nah I mean it was great, but that was the extent of its potential so I had to sell because here’s the next generational narrative… that they then end up rinsing and repeating over and over again.

So none of the names are great.

It’s constantly a dog chasing its tail.

And yes, more people get rinsed in the process.

But - what I believe is different right now on Robinhood Chain especially is that it’s a new chain.

That means new lore.

New opportunities to define narratives that transcend their way into the next bull market.

So - yes, you can still “have a traders mindset” and perform alright, but I think the majority of people who do have that mindset will get rinsed.

Vs. betting on narratives that can organically be carried by the growth of the chain itself take away all of the stress of trading and transform the mindset of dips into opportunities.

Because you actually believe in something.

So it all depends on where you think we are in this cycle especially with Robinhood Chain itself.

If you think it’s topped, Rasmr is probably right.

If you don’t on the other hand, find something you believe in that’s already had some solid distribution and momentum and just hold.

Murad only got his name for his conviction to hold.

And it worked for him.

I think he eventually should have been willing to take some off the table, but had he never believed in the first place he never would have been in the discussion of “oh what should he have done” because he would have gotten rid of those positions within the first four days of holding them.

People remember you for what you believe in.

If you believe in nothing, that’s what you’ll be remembered for, and you’ll probably end up with nothing in the process.

Neal wrote the argument Future Vision XPRIZE is built on: that science fiction stopped handing engineers something to build and started handing them only warnings.

Stephenson’s The Diamond Age (1995) is about an AI tutor that raises a child. 31 years later it's become the entire goal of AI education history. While he did not predict this outcome, he provided the blueprints to make it possible.

Snow Crash was a required reading for the Xbox team, it also inspired the inventors of Google Earth.

Out of one book real products were made by real engineers

Think about that, a word he made up was capable of reorganizing trillion-dollar companies.

The Future Vision XPRIZE finals will be hosted at Moonshots LIVE on Sep 25th in Los Angeles.

We’re asking filmmakers to do in three minutes what he’s done in novels for thirty years: describe a future so specific and so compelling that someone goes out and builds it.

He is exactly the right person to judge whether they pulled it off.

Rather than critiquing the problem, he founded Project Hieroglyph at Arizona State. Built on creating stories that inspire construction instead of fear. That’s the entire thesis of this prize.

here’s the best advice I’ve ever received:

“you need to stop thinking about it as money, and start thinking about it as time.”

please take 2 mins to read this because that bit of advice will dramatically change your quality of life.

it sounds silly when you start to think: 

“how much time am I spending to buy this?” instead of “how much money?”

but I’ll tell you why it’s not with the following example: 

the average car payment a month is £400 ($540) over a 5 year period.

the average car payment a month is 1 weeks worth of wages after tax a month.

the average person is trading 1/4 of their time every single month to drive a car.

how much would you pay to add an extra week to every single month? 

imagine the freedom you would have?

so why do we sell that time for £400?

because in doing so you’re selling the experiences and moments that might have been.

> time with your family
> time with your hobbies 
> time to learn something new
> time to focus on your health

you forego all of that when you sign that contract for a cheap dopamine hit for that new hot car with all the extra trimmings.

so start asking yourself “how much time am I spending to buy this?” from now on.

there’s other benefits that come from this as you liberate yourself from the burden of materialistic possession’s.

the things that you own will end up owning you. (bookmark it) 👇

A subscriber asked me: What do I read daily & who do I follow?

I will start with a few principles
1. A good writer isn't someone elaborate, or sophisticated. It's someone who can explain concepts simply, and someone you simply enjoy reading

2. It is far more important to choose what NOT to read, than what to read. You curate your diet. You don't eat junk foods. You don't consume too much sugar. Likewise, your mental diet has to be curated. You don't consume tabloids. You don't consume Tiktok slop 

3. Gell-Mann Amnesia: A cognitive bias where a person spots major errors in a news story about a topic they know well, but then reads the rest of the newspaper and trusts everything else as if it were completely accurate.

Hence, always read people who write about topics you know they're knowledgeable in

4. Lastly, consume broadly. I actually don't like reading Financial News that much, because it's my work. Instead, I get more value reading *non-financial* stuff. 

Now, my list:
1. @kylascan for Economics 
2. @PaulSkallas for esoteric wisdom
3. @robkhenderson for Sociology
4. @FT for financial-related news 
5. MicroCapClub & @howardmarks for investing
6. Fiction Books - Dune, LOTR, Enders Game, etc. Fiction books are really great for cognitive breaks 
7. @Noahpinion for economics
8. @agnostoxxx for trading
9. @kevinmuir for Macro

I think most software will be created by AI, and increasingly most software will also be consumed by AI on our behalf. So we’re going to see an explosion of software, not a reduction.

Looking at my own usage, I estimate that:

• For every web search I do, AI does 1,000x more
• For every email I send, AI sends 100x more
• For every SMS I send, AI sends 10x more
• For every spreadsheet I open, AI probably queries/manipulates 1000x more data behind the scenes

The conclusion is pretty simple: we should start building software for agents, because agents are going to become the primary users.
